summary: Login slowness and 503s on auth-service are caused by capacity saturation of auth-service under a genuine, externally-originated ~3.7x inbound traffic surge (H1, confidence 0.62): request_rate steps ~400 -> ~1,452 req/s in the same 06:52Z->06:54Z bucket as p99 (91ms -> 3.76s), error_rate (0.2% -> 11.7%) and CPU (~38% -> ~97%), with the only error signature being "accept queue full" 503s. The reported bcrypt-regression theory (H2) is rejected: there is no auth-service deployment in the window or the preceding three days, no request-path config change, and zero bcrypt log matches; the historical precedent HIST-101 required exactly such a bad deploy. Dependency-origin hypotheses (H3 shared-redis flood from portfolio-service v4.4.0, H4 downstream degradation) are contradicted by flat redis-cache CPU/memory and flat user-db CPU/slow-query metrics with no pre-06:52Z rise, plus a 64-minute quiet gap between the only deployment and onset. Confidence is capped rather than "inconclusive" because the remaining uncertainty concerns the identity of the traffic source and the unmeasurable kyc-provider path, not the location or mechanism of the failure.

ranked_hypotheses.title: Externally-driven login traffic surge saturates auth-service CPU/accept queue (capacity_saturation at auth-service)
ranked_hypotheses.statement: auth-service inbound request_rate steps from ~400 req/s to ~1,500 req/s at 06:54Z, pinning CPU at ~97% and overflowing the accept queue, which returns 503 'accept queue full' and inflates p99 to ~3.8s. Critically, the surge is externally-visible inbound demand, not an internal retry artifact: api-gateway's own inbound RPS rose in parallel (~1,244 -> ~4,763 req/s), and the gateway:auth RPS ratio stayed roughly constant (3.29 -> 3.14 -> 2.68), so auth-service is not re-requesting beyond the gateway's own traffic. Origin is auth-service capacity saturation under a genuine load spike; not a code regression.

causal_chain.claim: api-gateway inbound request_rate rises ~3.8x in the same sub-minute window (~1,244 req/s at 06:48Z -> 3,175 at 06:54Z -> 4,763 at 07:00Z), and auth-service's inbound rate tracks it (~385 -> 1,012 -> 1,814 req/s)

The gateway:auth RPS ratio stays roughly constant across onset (3.29 / 3.14 / 2.68), proving auth-service is not receiving ~3.7x the gateway's traffic and the surge is not a hidden retry/duplicate fan-out
auth-service CPU saturates at onset: ~37-38% baseline, partial rise at 06:36Z, then pinned at ~97% avg / ~99% max from 06:54Z onward
auth-service accept queue saturates; the only ERROR signature is queue saturation ('request rejected: accept queue full, returning 503' on POST /v1/auth/login), first seen 06:55:42Z
p99 latency and error_rate step up in the same 06:54Z bucket and remain elevated (~3.8s, ~14%)
Impact propagates upstream to api-gateway, whose p99 steps to ~3.9s in the same bucket — consistent with auth-service being the constraint
auth-service memory is flat across the window, so the saturation is CPU/queue-bound rather than a leak
No auth-service deployment (0 in window and preceding three days) and no request-path config change occurred; the log.level INFO->WARN change does not touch bcrypt or the hashing path
No bcrypt log signature exists (total_matched=0), so the reported bcrypt regression is not corroborated

assumptions: The load surge originates outside the observed services (external clients or an upstream caller not instrumented in this window); the rise in gateway inbound RPS is taken as the boundary of what we can measure, so the ultimate traffic source remains unidentified

Load precedes saturation: latency, error, CPU and request_rate all step within the same 06:36Z->06:54Z bucket, which is consistent with load-driven saturation but cannot be ordered below 2-minute resolution
auth-service's provisioned capacity cannot absorb ~1,500 req/s at its normal per-request CPU cost

ranked_hypotheses.title: A downstream dependency of auth-service (redis-cache / user-db / kyc-provider) degraded and auth-service is only where it surfaces
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A downstream component auth-service depends on degraded at/around onset, so login calls block on it and auth-service queues saturate. Tested against all available dependency telemetry: redis-cache CPU is flat across 06:30-07:10Z (no rise at or before 06:52Z), redis-cache memory is flat/normal, and user-db CPU (18.6, mean 18.0) and slow_queries_per_min (0.32, mean 0.31) are flat with no pre-06:52Z degradation. kyc-provider remains unmeasurable (no telemetry).

causal_chain.claim: A shared/external dependency of auth-service degrades around 06:5xZ
Login requests block on that dependency, inflating per-request latency
Blocked requests occupy workers until the accept queue overflows (503) and CPU rises to saturation
Latency/errors step up at auth-service and propagate to api-gateway

assumptions: kyc-provider has no telemetry at all (F24), so a kyc-provider-origin fault cannot be excluded by measurement and is the only surviving unfalsified branch of this hypothesis
A dependency latency regression could coincidentally coincide with a parallel 3.8x rise in both gateway and auth-service inbound RPS, which no plausible dependency fault mechanism would produce

ranked_hypotheses.title: portfolio-service v4.4.0 'Holdings export' floods the shared redis-cache, degrading auth-service transitively
ranked_hypotheses.statement: portfolio-service v4.4.0 added a CSV export endpoint at 05:50Z that hammers redis-cache (shared by auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine, market-data-service), slowing auth's cache lookups and producing the 3.8s p99 and 503s. Tested against telemetry: redis-cache CPU and memory are flat across 06:30-07:10Z with no step at or before 06:52Z, and there was a 64-minute quiet gap between the deploy and onset with no intervening config change.

causal_chain.claim: portfolio-service v4.4.0 (CSV 'Holdings export' endpoint) deploys at 05:50Z, live, not rolled back
The export endpoint generates heavy load against redis-cache, which is shared by all four services
redis-cache contention slows auth-service's cache-dependent login path
Slowed auth path backs up, CPU climbs and the accept queue overflows, yielding 3.8s p99 and 503 'accept queue full'

assumptions: The CSV export actually touches redis-cache heavily (no portfolio-service or redis-per-caller metrics were collected)
auth-service's login path materially depends on redis-cache for the slow part of each request
redis-cache contention would manifest as increased auth-service request volume rather than elevated per-request cache latency, and would leave redis-cache's own CPU at baseline 22%

ranked_hypotheses.title: Reporter's suspicion: bcrypt/hashing regression reintroduced in auth-service
ranked_hypotheses.statement: A new auth-service release reintroduced expensive hashing (as in HIST-101), causing per-login CPU burn, ~4s login latency and 503s. Rejected: no auth-service deployment exists in the window or the preceding three days, no bcrypt log messages exist, the sole error signature is accept-queue-full, and the step coincides with a parallel ~3.8x traffic rise at both gateway and auth-service.

causal_chain.claim: An auth-service deployment introduced a heavier bcrypt cost factor
Hashing cost raises per-request CPU, driving auth-service CPU to saturation
Saturated CPU produces 4s login p99 and 503s

assumptions: HIST-101's bcrypt signature is specific enough to recur identically
The absence of a deployment record is a telemetry gap rather than reality
ranked_hypotheses.rejection_reason: HIST-101's signature requires a bad auth-service deployment (F6); auth-service deployment count is 0 in the window and preceding three days (F2), with no request-path config change (F3). Zero bcrypt log matches in the onset window (F13); the only ERROR signature is accept-queue-full queue saturation, not hashing errors (F9). Degradation coincides with a parallel ~3.8x rise in BOTH gateway and auth-service inbound RPS with a constant ratio (F10, F14, F15, F16), which a fixed per-request hashing cost cannot produce.

facts.statement: auth-service p99 latency rises as a sharp step in the single 06:52Z->06:54Z bucket: 91.5ms at 06:52Z and 93.94ms at 06:50Z, then 3759.86ms at 06:54Z, sustained ~3.6-3.9s through 08:54Z with no gradual ramp.

auth-service memory_pct is flat across 06:30-07:10Z with no step at 06:52Z (mean 51.59, range 47.56-55.22), so the fault is CPU/queue-bound rather than memory-bound.
No auth-service deployment occurred in the window nor in the preceding three days (2026-04-18T00:00Z-2026-04-22T08:59Z): auth-service-scoped deployment count is 0.
The only config change across all services in the window is auth-service log.level INFO->WARN at 03:40Z ('Reduce log volume'), which does not touch bcrypt or the hashing/request path.
No bcrypt-related log messages exist in auth-service in the 06:50-08:59Z window: a WARN+ search for "bcrypt" returned total_matched=0.

The only deployment across all services in 2026-04-21T00:00Z-2026-04-22T08:59Z was portfolio-service v4.4.0 'Holdings export' at 05:50Z, status live, not rolled back.
redis-cache is shared by auth-service, portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service; kyc-provider is external with has_telemetry=false.
redis-cache cpu_pct is flat across 06:30-07:10Z with no rise at or before 06:52Z (mean 22.17, max 25.59), and memory_pct is flat/normal (mean 69.98, max 76.3) with no step at 06:52Z.
user-db cpu_pct is flat (mean 18.0, range 16.63-19.94) and slow_queries_per_min is flat (mean 0.31, range 0.18-0.51) with no pre-06:52Z degradation.
The quiet gap between the portfolio-service deploy at 05:50Z and the auth-service onset at 06:54Z is 64 minutes, with no config change in 05:00-07:10Z (config_changes count = 0 for all services).
kyc-provider has no telemetry at all (no logs/metrics) and can only be observed through its caller auth-service.

assumptions: The load surge originates outside the observed services (external clients or an upstream caller not instrumented in this window); the rise in api-gateway inbound RPS is taken as the boundary of what is measurable, so the ultimate traffic source remains unidentified.

Load precedes saturation: latency, error, CPU and request_rate all step within the same 06:36Z->06:54Z bucket, which is consistent with load-driven saturation but cannot be ordered below 2-minute resolution.
auth-service's provisioned capacity cannot absorb ~1,500 req/s at its normal per-request CPU cost.
The absence of any auth-service deployment record reflects reality rather than a telemetry gap; if deployment history were incomplete, a code-change origin could not be fully excluded.
The 372 truncated ERROR log entries are representative: only the accept-queue-full pattern is present, and no lower-severity context contradicts it.

A downstream dependency fault (e.g. kyc-provider) cannot be excluded by measurement because that component has no telemetry; it is excluded only indirectly, since auth-service's own CPU/queue saturates and the gateway and auth inbound rates rise in parallel — a pattern no plausible dependency fault would produce.

timeline.event: Only in-window config change: auth-service log.level INFO->WARN ('Reduce log volume'); does not touch bcrypt or the request/hashing path.
Only deployment across all services in the window: portfolio-service v4.4.0 'Holdings export' (CSV export endpoint), live, not rolled back.
Baseline: auth-service ~393-442 req/s, p99 ~91-94ms, error_rate ~0.19-0.27%, CPU ~37-38%; api-gateway p99 ~208-211ms, inbound RPS ~1,244.
First sign of change on auth-service CPU (avg 44.66, max 96.96) within the 06:36Z->06:54Z bucket.
Last near-baseline 60s sample: auth-service ~385 req/s, api-gateway ~1,244 req/s; gateway:auth ratio 3.29.
redis-cache cpu_pct 21.21 — at baseline immediately before the auth-service step; no dependency-side precursor.

Sharp step in the same bucket: auth-service p99 93.94ms -> 3759.86ms, error_rate 0.2% -> 11.72%, request_rate -> 1452.66 req/s, CPU pinned ~97%, rate_limited_per_min -> 451.86; api-gateway p99 -> 3908.96ms; redis-cache and user-db metrics remain flat.
First 'accept queue full' ERROR in auth-service logs, returning 503 on POST /v1/auth/login.
auth-service 1813.74 req/s with api-gateway 4859.74 req/s; gateway:auth ratio 2.68 — ratios remain in the same range as before onset.
api-gateway inbound RPS reaches ~4,763 req/s, confirming a sustained parallel inbound surge.
Incident INC-008 reported by on-call SRE (auth-service p99 3.8s, 503s on /v1/auth/login), framed as a suspected bcrypt regression as in HIST-101.
Last 'accept queue full' 503 in the observed window; auth-service p99, error_rate and CPU remain at saturated levels (last data 08:59Z).

recommended_actions.action: Immediately shed/limit load at the edge rather than restarting auth-service: apply or tighten rate limiting / traffic throttling on api-gateway for POST /v1/auth/login (the component already identified as carrying the surge) so auth-service inbound is brought back toward ~400-450 req/s, the level at which CPU was ~38% and p99 ~91ms.
recommended_actions.rationale: auth-service is CPU-pinned at ~97% with an overflowing accept queue producing 503s (F9, F11); the driver is inbound demand of ~1,452-1,814 req/s versus a ~400 req/s baseline (F10, F15). Reducing arrivals is the only lever that addresses the verified mechanism, and auth-service is refusing ~868-901 req/min already (F19).

recommended_actions.action: Do NOT roll back or hot-patch auth-service code as the primary mitigation (no auth-service deployment is present to roll back); if any release action is taken, treat it as capacity-driven, not code-driven.
recommended_actions.rationale: There is no auth-service deployment in the window or preceding three days (F2), no request-path config change (F3), and zero bcrypt log matches (F13); the HIST-101 playbook (rolling back a bad release) does not apply.

recommended_actions.action: Scale out / add capacity to auth-service (additional replicas or CPU headroom) and/or raise its accept-queue depth, so ~1.5k req/s can be absorbed at normal per-request cost, then verify p99 returns to ~90-200ms and error_rate to <0.5%.
recommended_actions.rationale: The verified failure mode is capacity saturation of auth-service (CPU ~97%, accept queue full), not a defect (F11, F9, F7, F8). Raising capacity directly addresses the mechanism.

recommended_actions.action: Identify and characterize the traffic source: enable per-client / per-route request attribution at api-gateway and auth-service, and confirm whether the parallel rise in gateway inbound RPS (~1,244 -> ~4,763 req/s) is genuine external client demand, a marketing/retry storm, or an upstream caller outside the instrumented boundary.
recommended_actions.rationale: The gateway:auth ratio stayed roughly constant (3.29/3.14/2.68), so the surge is externally-visible inbound demand and not an internal retry artifact (F16, F17, F14), but the ultimate origin is unidentified; gateway INFO+ logs for the onset window contained no 'auth' matches. Addressing or rate-limiting the source prevents recurrence of the same saturation.

recommended_actions.action: Keep the shared-cache and dependency paths closed out rather than pursued as active mitigations: no action on portfolio-service v4.4.0 or redis-cache/kyc-provider is warranted on current evidence.
recommended_actions.rationale: redis-cache CPU/memory are flat with no pre-06:52Z rise (F21, F22), user-db CPU and slow_queries are flat (F23), and there is a 64-minute quiet gap between the only deployment and onset with no intervening change (F28); the H3/H4 paths are contradicted by measurement.

recommended_actions.action: Add missing observability to close the residual blind spots: per-client/session request attribution for auth-service (no session/token metric today), latency/error metrics for redis-cache, user-db and kyc-provider, and inbound metrics for portfolio-service, pricing-engine and market-data-service.
recommended_actions.rationale: auth-service exposes no unique-login/session metric (F18); redis-cache and user-db expose no latency/error metrics; kyc-provider has no telemetry at all (F24). These gaps forced the investigation to infer dependency health indirectly from CPU/memory proxies.

recommended_actions.action: Establish capacity/load-shedding guardrails for auth-service: define a provisioned-RPS and CPU saturation threshold with automatic edge throttling and capacity alerts, and pre-agree the playbook branch 'load-driven saturation' vs 'bad release' so responders do not default to the bcrypt rollback playbook.
recommended_actions.rationale: This incident recurred in presentation to HIST-101 (F6) but had an entirely different mechanism; the acute need is preventing auth-service CPU-pinning under a ~3.7x inbound surge (F11, F10), and disambiguating the two signatures early.

data_gaps: The ultimate source of the traffic surge is unidentified: api-gateway INFO+ logs for 06:45-07:05Z containing 'auth' returned total_matched=0 and no per-client breakdown exists, so the gateway inbound rise (~1,244 -> ~4,763 req/s) marks the boundary of measurement rather than the origin.

auth-service exposes no session/token/unique-login metric (available: cpu_pct, error_rate, latency_p99_ms, memory_pct, rate_limited_per_min, request_rate, restarts), so a request-to-unique-session ratio could not be computed to positively separate distinct clients from duplicates.

Onset could not be pinned below the 2-minute (and, for some series, 60s) bucket, so whether load strictly precedes saturation is not demonstrated — only that all signals (latency, error, CPU, request_rate) step within the same 06:36Z->06:54Z bucket.

kyc-provider has no telemetry (has_telemetry=false) and can only be observed through auth-service, so a kyc-provider-origin dependency fault cannot be excluded by measurement — this is the only surviving unfalsified branch of H4.

redis-cache and user-db expose no latency_p99/error_rate metrics; only CPU/memory and counter-style proxies were available. redis hit_ratio_pct, evictions_per_min, user-db replication_lag_ms and connections_active were never retrieved (queries budget-exhausted), so a subtle no-CPU/no-memory cache or DB degradation cannot be fully ruled out.

No per-service request_rate or error signatures were pulled for portfolio-service, pricing-engine or market-data-service over 06:30-07:00Z, so the shared-cache/co-caller path (H3) could not be tested directly against those services' own traffic; it is contradicted only indirectly, via flat redis-cache and user-db metrics.
Blast radius beyond auth-service and api-gateway is unverified: no metrics for session-service or other peer services were retrieved (queries budget-exhausted).

Deployment and config-change history before 2026-04-21T00:00Z was not retrieved, and the 372 ERROR log entries were truncated (30 of 372 returned), so individual stack traces and lower-severity context around onset were not reviewed.
what_would_change_the_conclusion: Evidence that auth-service's ~3.7x request-rate rise is an internal retry/duplicate fan-out rather than genuine inbound demand — e.g. a per-client breakdown showing a small number of clients re-requesting, or gateway inbound RPS staying near baseline while auth-service spikes alone (would contradict F14/F16/F17 and re-open H4).

Discovery of an auth-service deployment or a request-path/feature-flag change activated near 06:54Z (e.g. within the un-scanned pre-2026-04-21 history or a staged rollout) would re-open the bcrypt/code-regression hypothesis (H2) despite F2/F3.
Any bcrypt- or hashing-related error/latency log signature in the truncated or lower-severity auth-service logs around onset (F13 currently shows total_matched=0).

A pre-06:52Z degradation in a dependency not measurable here — particularly kyc-provider (no telemetry at all) or a redis-cache/user-db signal in the unqueried counters (hit_ratio_pct, evictions_per_min, replication_lag_ms, connections_active) — would support H4 and shift the origin off auth-service capacity.

Evidence that portfolio-service v4.4.0's CSV export was driving heavy shared redis-cache traffic beginning before 06:52Z (e.g. elevated portfolio-service request_rate or redis evictions/hit-ratio degradation) would revive H3, notwithstanding the currently flat redis-cache CPU/memory and the 64-minute quiet gap.

Demonstration that ~1,500 req/s is within auth-service's designed capacity at its normal per-request CPU cost (i.e. the capacity assumption is wrong) would shift the diagnosis from capacity saturation toward a per-request cost regression or a hidden resource bottleneck.

The only config change across all services in the window is on auth-service: key log.level, INFO→WARN, at 2026-04-22T03:40:00Z, described as 'Reduce log volume' — it does not touch bcrypt or the hashing/request path.

Memory does not rise with the latency/error step — the auth-service fault is CPU/queue-bound, not memory.

redis-cache is the single shared component connecting all four services: edges auth-service->redis-cache, portfolio-service->redis-cache, pricing-engine->redis-cache, market-data-service->redis-cache all have kind 'cache', and redis-cache has shared=true. portfolio-service additionally calls market-data-service (http), which itself calls redis-cache — so portfolio-service and market-data-service also co-call each other.

portfolio-service v4.4.0 ('Holdings export', CSV export endpoint, status live, rolled_back_at=null) was deployed at 2026-04-22T05:50:00Z and is the only portfolio-service deployment in 2026-04-21T00:00Z–2026-04-22T08:59Z.

The quiet gap between the portfolio-service deploy (05:50Z) and the auth-service onset (06:54Z = first elevated bucket) is 64 minutes; there was no config change in 05:00–07:10Z to explain a trigger in between (config_changes count = 0 for all services).

Historical lead HIST-107 (2025-12-09, 'Cold cache storm after redis failover', services redis-cache + market-data-service) is a precedent for a shared redis-cache problem surfacing as downstream latency — but its root cause was a Redis primary failure/empty replica, a different mechanism from a single service flooding the cache. HIST-101 remains the only bcrypt precedent and it required a bad auth-service deploy, which is absent (F2).
